source.title: When Weak LLMs Speak with Confidence, Preference Alignment Gets Stronger
source.authors: Amirabbas Afzali; Myeong-Hwan Jeon; Maria Brbić

page_placements.theme: Properties other than accuracy under W2S: fairness, privacy, calibration, inherited data bias, interpretability

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Tests weak-model supervision for preference alignment and confidence-weighted training, but uses GRA and preference-optimization experiments rather than Burns et al.'s PGR measurement.
record.gate_note: The paper reports relevant weak-supervision and confidence-weighting results. It does not report PGR or directly compare the strong student's task performance with the weak annotator's performance. The weak annotator's own preference-label accuracy is not a matching student-versus-supervisor outcome, so it is not included as a row. Cited findings from Tao & Li and other work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: A new setting, weak-annotator preference alignment. A small LLM trained on human labels annotates preference pairs for a larger policy, and a training change (confidence weighting) is compared against naive weak-label DPO (WS-DPO). The measure is Gold Reward Accuracy against each model's own SFT baseline, not PGR. There is no strong ceiling and no comparison of student against supervisor, so V1 and V3 cannot be read. V2 (method gain over naive weak training) and one V4 failure mode (supervisor distribution shift, online vs offline) are tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that weighting weak-annotator preference labels by the annotator's confidence improves alignment over naive weak labels (WS-DPO) and over human labels on average (about +5 GRA). They also report that CW-DPO with 20-30% human labels beats DPO on 100% human labels. In appendices they report failure online under distribution shift and degradation when the weak annotator is trained on biased or poisoned data. They require the annotator to be aligned with the target preference.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a preference-annotator setup with Bradley–Terry-trained weak models and confidence-weighted DPO/IPO/rDPO; evaluates Gold Reward Accuracy rather than Burns et al.'s performance gap recovered.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with student size, dataset/task, preference objective, confidence threshold versus weighting, and offline versus online data regime. The authors also report sensitivity to the balance and poisoning of weak-annotator training data.

fits_no_version.finding: When the weak annotator's training labels are poisoned (5-20%) or skewed between Harmless and Helpful, the strong student's GRA degrades along the bias. CW-DPO degrades less than WS-DPO at 10-20% poisoning but not at 5%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weak-to-strong students inherit systematic biases in the weak supervisor's training data; confidence weighting only partly buffers this.

record.problems: Main experiments are reported as single runs; a later appendix reports standard deviations over three disjoint test subsets for selected results. GRA is measured against an SFT baseline and does not establish student-versus-supervisor performance or PGR. Several evaluation results rely on reward models, and the paper's online and poisoning results do not quantify PGR.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 full-human comparisons; Table 5 alternative weighting functions; Table 6 weak annotator training-objective accuracy/time; Tables 16-20 and 23-26 additional cross-family, judge, variance, domain, or annotator-design analyses; figures and qualitative examples. These were omitted to prioritize main WS-DPO comparisons, student-size results, confidence filtering, distribution-shift tests, and biased-data tests within the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No comparison of the student's performance against the weak supervisor's, no strong ceiling, no PGR. The weak annotator's accuracy (Table 6, about 64%) is on a different task from the student's GRA.

GRA is relative to each student's SFT baseline, and the authors say it is not comparable across sizes. Weak-size effects (Table 12) cover annotator accuracy only. Nothing on what predicts weak-to-strong gains.
Students exploiting what the supervisor can't check, and gains shrinking when weak and strong models err alike: not tested.

missing.what: Confidence filtering vs naive use of all weak labels (top 30% vs 100%). Top 30% beats 100% in all six conditions, e.g. OPT Harmless 72.3 vs 67.4 and Qwen HH-RLHF 71.3 vs 63.2. This is a method gain over naive weak training.

record.verdict_notes: GRA is a win rate against each student's own SFT model, judged by an external reward model, so no PGR can be computed. Main results are single runs, and many CW-vs-WS differences fall within the Table 20 SDs. Important result in rows_left_out: Table 16 (cross-family) shows CW-DPO below WS-DPO in all three conditions for OPT-125M→Qwen-2.5-14B (66.4 vs 72.2, 55.9 vs 57.2, 77.7 vs 79.7). It is also below WS-DPO on one of three conditions for Qwen-0.5B→Llama-8B (66.2 vs 67.2). This further limits V2 and should be added as rows, although the authors report a 3.3% average gain. The authors frame their setting as distinct from classic weak-to-strong, because the weak supervisor can outperform human labels.

versions.untested_parts: No direct comparison of student performance against weak-supervisor performance and no PGR or strong-ceiling measurement.
Tests confidence weighting against weak-supervised DPO and confidence filtering in preference alignment; does not establish PGR gains.
Reports GRA across student sizes and preference datasets/tasks, but not PGR; does not isolate the effect of weak-supervisor size on student PGR or examine representations/what predicts PGR.

Tests online distribution mismatch and biased/poisoned weak-annotator training data. Does not test students exploiting supervisor blind spots or whether gains shrink when weak and strong models err alike.
No theoretical conditions requiring a student to beat its supervisor.
Language-model preference alignment only; no vision experiments.

relationships.condition: Offline CW-IPO, CW-rDPO, and CW-DPO on small and mid-sized OPT/Qwen students (1.3B-13B) on HH-RLHF, TL;DR and UFB
relationships.reason: Confidence weighting raises GRA over naive weak-label training by about 3-15 points in these conditions (R01,R02,R05-R09,R13,R15,R16,R19,R21-R25,R27-R33), and beats the best confidence-filtering threshold (R39,R40).
relationships.display_finding: Confidence weighting increased GRA by about 3–15 points over naive weak-label training and exceeded the best tested confidence-filtering threshold.

source_check.condition: Offline CW-IPO, CW-rDPO, and CW-DPO on small and mid-sized OPT/Qwen students (1.3B-13B) on HH-RLHF, TL;DR and UFB
source_check.reason: Tables 1–2 show clear method gains in the cited successful settings; Table 4 supports weighting over filtering. These are GRA gains, not measured PGR gains. The cited evidence also includes successful IPO/rDPO results at Qwen2.5-14B, outside the written size range.

relationships.condition: CW-DPO on the largest students (Qwen2.5-14B, and OPT-13B on UFB), and the online iterative setting
relationships.reason: Gain is nil or under 2 points for 14B and OPT-13B UFB (R03,R10,R11,R12,R20,R34), matching the authors' 'gains diminish' remark. Online, CW-DPO does not beat WS-DPO on HH-RLHF (R41, 55.1 vs 56.3) and is only +2.1 on TL;DR (R42).
relationships.display_finding: Gains were zero or under 2 points for Qwen2.5-14B and OPT-13B on UFB; online CW-DPO scored 55.1 versus WS-DPO's 56.3 on HH-RLHF and gained 2.1 on TL;DR.
